# Cadence — task list

The running record of work: open, in progress, done, cancelled. Started 2026-08-16.

**Format.** One line per item: `- [id] Title — note`. Ids are stable and never reused, so a
cancelled or done item can still be referenced later. Done items keep their commit sha, because the
commit message is where the *reasoning* lives; this file is only the index.

**Rule (set 2026-08-17).** *Every* request the user makes lands here the moment it is made, whether
or not work starts on it — under **In progress** if it is being worked now, otherwise under the
right Open section. An item moves to **Done** only when the code behind it is committed (or
otherwise verified), not when it is written.

**Target devices** (set 2026-08-16). Build and verify for these three only; anything that exists
solely to serve other hardware is dead weight and should be removed rather than maintained:

| Device | Points | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| iPhone 15 (base) | 393 × 852 | compact width, the only phone shape that matters |
| iPad Pro 11" | 834 × 1210 portrait · 1210 × 834 landscape | pane = window − 188pt sidebar → **646** portrait, **1022** landscape |
| MacBook Pro 14" | 1512 × 982 | the macOS surface |

Both iPad panes matter to Today's layout: 646pt portrait falls **below**
`CadenceTodayLayoutSupport.twoPaneMinimumWidth` (761), so portrait is one column and landscape is
two. The three-pane floor of 1022pt that this note used to cite is gone with the layout itself
(T-06).

- [T-5561] **OPEN 2026-10-23 (agent `macsearch`, the commit carrying this line; found while landing [[T-3084]]'s second half) -- the owner's "lists first, then tasks" has a second reading that [[T-3084]] did not implement: should a list DOCUMENT rank above tasks, and if so, where?** The decision as recorded reads "**lists first, then tasks.** Containers rank above their contents, so searching a list's name returns the list as the top hit rather than burying it under thirty of its own tasks. Not one-section-per-kind." [[T-3084]] implemented the reasoning sentence literally: a CONTAINER is an Area or a Project, its CONTENTS are its tasks, and `buildIndexedSource` already orders Areas and Projects before Tasks -- now pinned by `CadenceMacListDocumentSearchTests.containersRankAboveTheirContents`, which dies if that order moves. **The other reading is that the new list-document rows themselves belong above Tasks.** A list document is not a container of tasks, so the reasoning sentence does not reach it; but the palette's Notes section is drawn LAST, after Tasks, so a list document matching the same query as fourteen of its list's tasks is listed below all of them. **Why this is an owner question and not an implementer's call:** the palette is a fixed sequence of per-category sections (`GlobalSearchIndexSupport.buildIndexedSource` appends Commands, Pages, Areas, Projects, Tasks, Calendar Events, Event Notes, Notes, and `GlobalSearchOverlayStateSupport.keyboardRows` walks them in that order). Lifting list documents above Tasks therefore needs EITHER a new section ordered before `.tasks` -- which is the one-section-per-kind the same decision rules out -- OR moving the whole Notes section above Tasks, which would move Daily, Weekly and Notepad rows too, a visible change to four kinds that nobody asked for. **What is wanted here is one answer, not a design:** (a) leave it as landed -- list documents sit in the Notes section, containers stay above their contents; (b) list documents get their own section above Tasks, accepting the per-kind section; or (c) the whole Notes section moves above Tasks, accepting that the other four kinds move with it. Nothing is broken either way -- this is ranking, not discovery, and discovery works. Filed rather than guessed because the decision says the ranking is "explicitly not left to the implementer".

  `weekStartDate(forWeekKey:calendar:)` reads the *caller's*, so the pair only round-trips east of

  week, all 400 iterations. Two findings, and the second is the more expensive one.
  **1. The API asymmetry.** `weekStartDate(forWeekKey:calendar:)` sets `iso.timeZone =
  calendar.timeZone` — deliberate, and the whole point of `c424f42`. `weekKey(from:)` builds its own
  `Calendar(identifier: .iso8601)` two declarations above and **never sets a time zone**, so it
  silently takes the device's. Hand it the Monday-00:00-**UTC** that `weekStartDate` just returned
  for a UTC calendar and a Mac west of UTC calls that instant *Sunday*, i.e. the previous ISO week.
  Measured here by direct computation outside the test host, mirroring both helpers: 400/400
  mismatches under `America/Los_Angeles` and `America/New_York`, **0/400** under `Asia/Shanghai`,
  `Europe/London` (BST) and `Pacific/Auckland`.

  changed between the green runs and this red one; the Mac's time zone did. `c424f42` was authored
  at `+0800`, where the round-trip is exact, so the test recorded the sum of a real API asymmetry and
  the author's longitude and reported it as a pass. A test that only passes east of UTC is an
  instrument blind to its own environment — it was never measuring the property it names. Note also
  that `TZ=…` does **not** reach the spawned macOS test host: `TZ=Asia/Shanghai` and
  `TZ=America/Los_Angeles` produce byte-identical 400-failure runs, so the zone cannot be varied
  from the outside and the correction has to be that both halves take a calendar.
  **Not a user-facing defect, verified rather than assumed.** `DateFormatters.ymd` pins a locale and
  no time zone, so `date(from:)` parses to *local* midnight; every shipping caller of the week
  helpers therefore stands in the device zone on both sides and agrees with itself. Enumerated at
  `8c45c91`: `NotesView.swift:262`, `CadenceNoteDateNavigation.weekRangeLabel`/`weekKey(forDayKey:)`,
  `CadenceNotesListSupport:356`, `CadenceMCPServiceSupport:40`, and `currentWeekKey()` — every one
  takes the `.current` default, and the two declarations that *do* accept a `calendar:`
  (`CadenceNoteDateNavigation.title`, `weekRangeLabel`) are never handed a non-current one outside
  the tests. **This matters because `weekKey` output is persisted** (`Note.weekKey`,
  `WeeklyNote.weekKey`) and syncs through CloudKit, in Production since 2026-09-05: no stored key may
  change meaning, so the fix must be default-preserving.
  **The fix:** give `weekKey` the courtesy `weekStartDate` already has —
  `weekKey(from:calendar: Calendar = .current)` setting `cal.timeZone = calendar.timeZone` — and have
  the test pass its `utc` calendar to both halves of the round-trip.

- [T-2085] **CLOSED 2026-10-06 (agent `runstate`) — both halves fixed, and the second one is fixed so that it cannot recur rather than by anybody remembering to check first.** The diagnosis in this entry is correct in every particular and I reproduced it deliberately before fixing it. **(1) THE BUDGET.** Root `AGENTS.md` is **199 lines by `wc -l` / 200 by the test's count**, against the 200 the test allows, and the byte count is 14004 of 18000. The eight-line triage bullet `1d8786cd` added is **one line** now — HEAD's own first line of it, kept verbatim, which is also what proves the reconstruction was rebuilt on HEAD rather than on the revision before it ([[T-1246]]'s escape from `REBUILD-BEHIND-HEAD`, taken instead of `--commits-stale`) — and its seven lines of detail moved to `docs/AGENTS_REFERENCE.md` under *"Telling a queued run from a wedged one (moved out of AGENTS.md, 2026-10-06)"*, which is the pattern [[T-1391]]/[[T-1392]] documents and which that file already carries five of. `lineBudget` was NOT raised. **Worth knowing: there is now ZERO headroom.** The file was 198 lines before `1d8786cd` and is 199 now, so the next line anybody adds to root `AGENTS.md` fails this test; the next addition there has to displace something, which is what the budget is for. **(2) THE RUNNER REWRITTEN UNDERNEATH ITSELF, REPRODUCED IN ISOLATION FIRST.** A four-line zsh script was truncated and rewritten with forty lines one second into its own `sleep`: it ran its own four lines and then executed **thirty-six lines that were never part of its program**. That is `zsh` reading a script incrementally by byte offset into one open fd, and it is exactly `xcb-widgetdrop-tests` re-running its whole test phase. **It happened a SECOND time, to this entry's own cause.** `1d8786cd`'s author appended ~60 lines to `scripts/xcb.sh` at 01:52 while their own verification run was in postflight; that run had already printed its complete `== xcb result ==` block and was found 40 minutes later executing `test-host-lock.sh acquire` **as a child of itself**, holding the test-host lock and queued behind it at the same time, with `uiseed` and `precheck` stuck behind that. Killed, the lease reclaimed on owner-death, and `uiseed` took the lock 16 seconds later. **THE FIX IS THE ONE THIS ENTRY SUGGESTED**, at the top of `scripts/xcb.sh`: the runner copies itself to `${TMPDIR}cadence-xcb-self.<pid>.<n>.zsh`, re-execs from the copy, and **unlinks the copy immediately** — the fd stays valid (probed), so there is no path left for anyone to edit and no litter either. `exec` keeps the pid, which is what the log name and the lock ticket are keyed on, and `SCRIPT_PATH`/`ROOT_DIR` are carried across explicitly so `$here` and `$ROOT_DIR/scripts/test-host-lock.sh` keep naming the real checkout. It **fails open**: a runner that will not start because it could not copy itself would be worse than one that can be edited underneath it. **PROVED BY INDUCING THE REAL FAILURE, WITH THE CONTROL THAT MAKES IT EVIDENCE.** `xcb.sh selftest` section 14 (6 checks; 209 → 215 total, all green) starts a real `xcb.sh <id> test` against stubs and, while it is inside xcodebuild, **truncates and rewrites its own script file in place** with ~900 KB of injected program — far longer than the script, so the read offset cannot land past EOF. Guarded: no injected text, exactly ONE `== xcb result` block, postflight reached, no snapshot left behind, and **no zsh diagnostic naming its own script**. The CONTROL is the same scenario with the guard switched off, and it really does corrupt — it printed `…/ctl/scripts/xcb.sh:21756: unmatched "`, the same shape as `widgetdrop`'s `./scripts/xcb.sh:3336: command not found: the`. Mutating the guard away kills the diagnostic check. **AND THE OTHER HALF OF THE LESSON, which this entry does not state and which every agent needs: HOW you write the file decides whether this can happen at all.** `open(path, "w")` and an in-place editor truncate the SAME inode, which is what hijacks a running shell; writing a temp file on the same filesystem and `mv`-ing it over the target is a rename, leaves the running process's inode untouched, and is atomic. Measured both ways in one probe: the in-place form made the running script execute 36 foreign lines, the rename form left it printing its own three. **Every edit to `scripts/xcb.sh` in this commit was installed by rename while `uiseed` was executing the old copy, and `uiseed` was unaffected.**

What is left is LATENCY, not loss, and it is [[T-3152]].** **The filing (2026-10-11, read-only audit, agent `auditdata`) was exact about the coverage gap and wrong about the consequence.** `CadenceStoreSupport.makeSharedWriteContainer()` does default to `cloudKitDatabase: .none` and does open the same `default.store` the app opens with `.private("iCloud.com.haoranwei.Cadence")`; reachability is verified (`CadenceWidgets/TodayTasksWidgetView.swift:432` draws `Button(intent: CompleteTaskIntent(...))` and `CadenceAppShortcuts` exposes `CaptureTaskIntent` to Siri, both `perform()`ing in the extension); and `CadenceWidgets/CadenceWidgets.entitlements` still carries no `icloud-container-identifiers`. But the *consequence* was borrowed whole from a sentence written about the MCP server at `CadenceModelContainerFactory.swift:24-37`, under the still-open [[T-3018]]: *"a container with mirroring off does not maintain the mirroring metadata the app's own container exports from, so a write that lands through this door may never reach the owner's other devices and may not register there as a change at all."* **That sentence names the wrong mechanism.** **MEASURED, locally, with no CloudKit call, no owner store touched and no app-group path composed.** A SwiftData store opened with `ModelConfiguration(cloudKitDatabase: .none)` writes `ATRANSACTION`/`ACHANGE` rows on every save — two saves gave two transactions and two changes, read back both through `sqlite3` on a scratch store under the session scratchpad and through SwiftData's own `fetchHistory(HistoryDescriptor<DefaultHistoryTransaction>())`. A **separate, read-only** container over the same file reads those transactions, so the stream is not private to the writer. Every transaction carries `author == nil`: a widget write announces nothing, so **nothing in the stream a mirroring delegate consumes distinguishes it from a write the app itself made**. `bundleIdentifier` is the one field that differs between the two processes, and no export is known to filter on it. Per-record CloudKit metadata is written by the *exporting* container when it exports; a row another process inserted arrives at that pass in exactly the state a row the app inserted arrives in. **WHAT LANDED.** `CadenceSharedStoreWriteGateTests.aWidgetWriteThroughTheMirroringOffGateEntersTheStoresPersistentHistory` drives the **shipping path** — `CaptureTaskIntent.captureTask` then `CompleteTaskIntent.completeTask`, over a container from the real `makeSharedWriteContainer` gate, in a fresh temporary directory — and asserts the insert and the update each appear as a transaction read back through a separate read-only container, with `author == nil` throughout. That `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer`'s export is driven by this history stream is platform behaviour taken from outside this tree, not measured. *When* the owner's app next runs an export pass over a widget's transaction is unmeasured — [[T-2010]] records that even the *delivery* of a mirroring event needs a two-device run, and [[T-1309]] is this repository's one nearby observation (a phone signed without the push entitlement picked up the Mac's edits only when it happened to relaunch). (1) The extension's writes go through `CadenceStoreSupport.makeSharedWriteContainer()` in `Cadence/Services/CadenceWidgetIntents.swift` (`CompleteTaskIntent.perform`, `CaptureTaskIntent.perform`), whose `cloudKitDatabase:` defaults to `.none`; its reads (`CadenceWidgets/TodayTasksWidget.swift`, `CadenceWidgets/CalendarSnapshotWidget.swift`) pass `.none` explicitly. (2) `CadenceWidgetIntents.swift` sits under `Cadence/`, the `Cadence` app target's `PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup` (its exception set excludes only `Info.plist` and the `AGENTS.md` files), AND is listed in the `CadenceWidgets` Sources phase -- so both intents are app code too, reachable from Shortcuts while the app runs and from the `CadenceTests` host. Passing `.private("iCloud.com.haoranwei.Cadence")` at those call sites would, in the app process, open a second mirroring container over the `default.store` that `PersistenceController` already mirrors. The change is therefore not confined to the extension, and [[T-3152]]'s scope said to stop and file rather than widen. **What a fix has to decide:** a per-process switch (mirror only when running inside the `.appex`), or moving the intents out of the app target -- which changes what Shortcuts lists ([[T-2078]] records that a compiled-in intent is a Shortcuts action whether or not a widget draws it). **Also unmeasured, and each could sink the approach:** (a) whether two processes mirroring one store file at once is safe -- the app and the extension would each hold a mirroring delegate over the same persistent history; (b) whether a short-lived intent process lives long enough after `perform()` returns for an export to finish; (c) whether the sandboxed macOS extension needs `com.apple.security.network.client`, which both app files carry and `CadenceWidgets.entitlements` does not; (d) the widget extension's memory ceiling with mirroring set up in-process. `CadenceStoreSupport.makeSharedWriteContainer`'s doc comment says the extension "carries no `icloud-container-identifiers`"; that goes stale when [[T-3152]]'s entitlement lands and should change in the same commit as this fix. Do not add a second writer."* (exit 3), and the refusal is RIGHT -- a second writer on the CloudKit-backed app-group store has hung instances and needed a force-quit, once for 15 hours. - [T-3234] **OPEN 2026-10-19 (filed by agent `t3229` at coordinator instruction, out of a MEASURED collision the same day; a tooling/process defect, not a product bug) -- the ledger is a file-based id allocator and parallel worktrees break it, because "the next free id" is only true in the worktree that asks.** **The mechanism.** Ticket ids are allocated by appending a `- [T-NNNN]` line to `docs/TODO.md`, and an agent picks the next number by reading its own checkout -- `./scripts/ledger-view.sh show` and a `grep` over `docs/TODO.md` / `docs/TODO_DONE.md` both read the WORKING TREE. An agent on an isolated `post23/*` worktree therefore cannot see an id a sibling has already committed on its own branch, nor one committed to `main` after its branch point. The repo's standing rule -- *file the id before quoting it* -- was written for this exact hazard, but it only serialises writers who share one checkout; it assumes one writer and does not survive parallel worktrees. **And the tooling very nearly already does.** `agent-commit.sh` DOES parse `- [T-NNNN]` ids at commit time -- renumbering this very entry was refused with `LEDGER-IDS-LOST: this commit drops ledger entries HEAD has: T-3232`, which had to be acknowledged with `--drops-ids`. So the id parser, the refusal path and the override flag all exist already. **The gap is the DIRECTION of the comparison:** it asks "does this commit LOSE an id HEAD has" and never asks "does this commit ADD an id something else already has". One is a reconstruction guard, the other is an allocation guard, and only the first was written. **And the first is not thin, which is what makes the absence of the second striking:** retiring this one id walked through THREE escalating refusals in a row -- `LEDGER-IDS-LOST` wanting `--drops-ids`, then a second asking whether the entry was being archived or struck off and wanting `--retires-ids`, each one making the agent name what it meant. A commit that INVENTS a colliding id passes all of them without a word. **One of those refusals, `LEDGER-ID-UNFILED`, even names this outcome in its own text** -- *an id that lives only in a commit message is invisible to the next agent computing "next free", which is how one id went to two agents in a single week*. **Do not read that as already covering this.** Its model is an id that was never FILED, and its remedy is to write the stub into `docs/TODO.md`. Both colliding T-3232s were filed, properly, as formal ledger entries in `docs/TODO.md`, each committed before being quoted -- exactly as that guard demands. They collided anyway, because the guard asks whether an id is written down and the hazard is WHERE it is written down. Filing an id in an isolated worktree makes it visible to the filer and to nobody else. **The measured instance.** On 2026-10-19 agents `t3229` and `t3230` both allocated **T-3232**, in the same window, from different worktrees: `t3230`'s was the calendar glyph's chroma exceeding the rail's, `t3229`'s was the capture card seeding its `.onDate` end with the draft's start day. Both agents were correct to file and neither could see the other. `t3230`'s landed on main first at `67a83522`; `t3229`'s was renumbered to [[T-3233]] by coordinator instruction. **Two candidate fixes, and the second is the one the tooling could actually make.** (1) *Allocate from `main` only, through the coordinator* -- correct, and it costs a round trip per id, which is the whole reason agents allocate for themselves. (2) **Have `agent-commit.sh` refuse a `- [T-NNNN]` line whose id already exists on `main` or on ANY `post23/*` or `codex/*` branch** -- the same parse it already runs, pointed outward instead of backward, with a `--claims-id` style acknowledgement beside the `--drops-ids` that already exists. The data is local and the check is cheap -- `git show <ref>:docs/TODO.md` over every such ref, which measured at 28 branches plus main on 2026-10-19, the sweep that cleared T-3233 and T-3234 for this entry and left T-3235 verified free beside them -- and it fires at COMMIT time, which is exactly when the rule says the id becomes real. It turns a silent collision discovered at landing into a refusal the filing agent can act on. **Checking only `main` is what produced this** and must not be the fix: `t3229`'s id was free on main at the moment it was chosen. The check has to span branches. **Note for whoever takes it:** a refusal needs to name the branch and the colliding title, or the agent cannot tell a real clash from its own branch being read twice. More members than minutes collapses some slices, so those members share a start and their relative order falls to the overlap solver's tie-break; that is the one ordering promise the pass does not make, and it says so. **No member's `estimatedMinutes` is rewritten** — an estimate is user data that Focus, planning totals and an hours-mode `Goal` read; a migration may move a start, it may not invent a duration. - [T-3184] **CLOSED 2026-10-16 (agent `compactcascade`, the commit carrying this line; SEEN ON SCREEN on `Cadence-iPhone15` and MUTATION-PROVEN on a scratch copy) — a compact day column cascades every kind with the later start in front, and the block behind can never be covered edge to edge.** `iOSCalendarTimelineBlockLayout.Kind.mayCascade(isCompactWidth:)` answers `isCompactWidth || self == .event`, so at compact width a task, a bundle and an event all cascade under [[T-3161]]'s one rule — later start in front, no kind-based precedence anywhere — while at regular width the solver's answer is byte-for-byte [[T-3165]]'s column split. Bundles are wired EXACTLY as tasks are: the kind reaches the solver as one `Bool` and nothing new is built on `TaskBundle` ([[T-3170]]). **"Compact" is the HORIZONTAL SIZE CLASS**, which the owner named as the idiomatic answer and which is taken: `iOSCalendarTimelineGrid` already resolves it for the hour rail and the column width, so it is handed down as `isCompactWidth:` and the column never reads it again. A point threshold would need a constant nobody has measured and would need re-measuring for every pane the calendar appears in; the size class survives a narrow iPad Split View for free. **Draw order had to move with it, and that half is what would have reintroduced the bug.** macOS gets "later start in front" free — one array sorted by start minute at one `zIndex`, and only events cascade. The iOS column draws three `ForEach`es, bundles then events then tasks, so a task was painted over every event in the column whatever the clock said; a task that cascades under that z order is drawn BEHIND the event it indented past and the event is repainted full width across it, which is [[T-3165]]'s overpaint out of the fix for it. `iOSCalendarTimelineBlockLayout.zIndexes(for:)` now gives every block a z off the solver's own start order (ties by input order), and the draft layer and the now-line take `overlayZIndex` above them. **The negative is enforced by arithmetic rather than by measurement.** `cascadeIndent` could return **zero** on a slot at or under `minimumCascadedWidth`, which is a "cascade" that covers the block behind edge to edge. `CadenceCalendarOverlapLayout.minimumVisibleLeadingEdge` is **4pt** — `CadenceCalendarEventStyle.railWidth` plus the 1pt `strokeBorder` both block bodies draw, so the whole leading marker survives — and it now OUTRANKS the squeeze ceiling, with a half-slot cap so neither block can vanish on a pinched column. The indent is therefore strictly inside `0 ..< slotWidth` for every depth and every width, swept 1.0–400.0pt against depths 1–12 by `noCascadedBlockEverCoversTheOneBehindIt`. None of the eight is on the Codex lease. **The shape, from the mocks:** a Task/Event switch at the top that repaints the draft block live ([[T-3160]]'s `rail*` for an event, `plate*` for a task); title; a date-and-time row that collapses to one line and expands to all-day, separate start and end DATES so a block can span days, and repeat; kind-specific rows (location and calendar for an event; list, priority, estimate for a task); a notes field; and Cancel / Save, with Delete present only when editing. Creating and editing differ by whether the record exists and by that one button — not by being different screens. **Two picker rulings from the owner, and one of them is new work:** the date selector must be **Cadence's own** — `Cadence/Shared/Components/CadenceDatePicker.swift` already exists and is the grid to use, NOT a system `DatePicker`. The time selector must be **a roller that rolls hour and minute SEPARATELY**, and **nothing like it exists in the tree**: a sweep for `WheelDatePickerStyle`, `.wheel` and hour/minute pickers returns nothing, and `Cadence/Shared/Components/CadenceStartTimeFieldRow.swift` takes a flat `@Binding var minutes: Int`. So the roller is a new shared component, and it belongs in `Shared/Components` beside the date picker because both platforms need it. **Why this is worth the size:** the same four fields are currently spelled four times, which is how [[T-3160]]'s swap had to touch so many paint sites and how the iPad timeline ([[T-3169]]) ended up able to create only a task. One panel means the next change to what a task HAS is one edit. **Sequencing:** [[T-3169]] is building the iPad create panel now and is the first instance of this shape — it should be written as the shared panel from the start rather than retrofitted, and this ticket then adopts it at the other seven sites. Secondary, and weaker: a declined-hunk record whose lines sit inside the same declaration the commit is rewriting should refuse rather than decline. [[T-3100]] [[T-781]]

Hardcoding yellow over it would break the picker for all nine destinations. **Reset IS reachable, on macOS:** Settings → Sidebar → Today → the amber swatch, because `CadenceColorPalette.destinationTints` is `Theme`'s own six accents and T-245 made it so precisely to stop a default becoming unreachable. **It is NOT reachable on iOS** — `iOSSidebarLayoutSettingsSection` reorders and hides rows and only *reads* the tint — so an iPad- or iPhone-only user has no way back. - [T-3088] **CLOSED 2026-10-09 (agent `monthpriority`, the commit carrying this line) — on an overfull month-grid day the calendar EVENTS take the chip slots and the TASKS overflow into "+N more", on both platforms, through one shared function.** **THE SURVEY FIRST, because the two platforms did not agree and the Mac was the one that was wrong.** macOS's `MonthDayCell` (`Cadence/macOS/Views/CalendarPageMonthSupportViews.swift`) derived a slot count from the row height it was given (`CalendarMonthCellLayout.chipLayout`) and then filled it `bundles.prefix(layout.visible)` -> `tasks.prefix(remaining)` -> `events.prefix(remaining)`: **events were LAST**, so a crowded day hid its events and kept its tasks, and it drew the task chips above the event chips to match. iOS's `iOSCalendarMonthDayCell` (`Cadence/iOS/iOSCalendarMonthViews.swift`) was already events-before-tasks, but through three hardcoded per-kind caps — `bundles.prefix(3)`, `events.prefix(max(0, 4 - bundles))`, `tasks.prefix(max(0, 5 - bundles - events))` — over a fixed five-slot cell rather than a measured one. So **one platform had the rule, neither stated it, and no line of either was reachable from the other**; the answer was insertion order on one side and three interlocking literals on the other. **THE OWNER'S REASONING, recorded on the type rather than here:** an event is a time-bound commitment you cannot reschedule unilaterally, so a hidden event costs the reader more than a hidden task, which can move without asking anybody; and it is the ranking Apple Calendar and Fantastical already trained the user on. **THE FIX** is `CadenceCalendarMonthCellPriority.split(bundles:events:tasks:capacity:)` in `Cadence/Shared/`, called by both cells and by nothing else. It returns a per-kind `Split` of counts rather than items, because macOS holds `CalendarEventItem`s and iOS holds `EKEvent`s and the ordering is a fact about the *kinds*. **Capacity stays each platform's own** and deliberately so: macOS's is derived from the row height (minus the slot the "+N more" label takes), the iPhone's is a fixed `chipCapacity = 5` because those rows have a `minHeight` and no budget to divide. How many rows there are is a layout question; who gets them is this one. **Bundles keep the rank both platforms already gave them** — a bundle is the shape of the day rather than one of its items, and the owner's argument ranks events against *tasks*. **TWO THINGS CHANGED BEYOND THE ORDERING, both stated rather than slipped in.** (1) macOS now draws its event chips ABOVE its task chips, so the surviving chips read top-down as what matters most and the two platforms draw the same order; pinned by `theMacMonthCellDrawsEventChipsAboveTaskChips`. (2) iOS loses its per-kind sub-caps, so a day with five events and no bundles now draws five event chips where it drew four and a task. That is the sub-caps being the drift rather than the rule: a second spelling of a priority is what the two cells had, and keeping one platform's arbitrary 3-and-4 would have meant the shared function taking per-platform parameters, which is the same drift wearing a parameter list. **The "+N more" count now comes off the same `Split` that produced the chips** (`split.hidden`, not a second subtraction), so the chips and the number above them cannot describe different days. **MUTATION-PROVEN.** `split`'s fill order reversed to tasks-before-events (the `drawnEvents`/`drawnTasks` pair swapped): it COMPILED, and was killed by `CalendarMonthCellPriorityTests.anOverfullMonthDayDrawsItsEventsAndOverflowsItsTasks` and `.whenEventsAloneOverflowTheCellNoTaskTakesASlotFromThem`. Restored byte-identical from a `cp` backup. **The test asserts the PARTITION, not the remainder**, which is the whole point: a day of three events and six tasks in four slots has a remainder of five under either ordering, so `#expect(hidden == 5)` alone is green for the behaviour this ticket was filed about. **Green:** macOS `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 warnings; iOS `generic/platform=iOS Simulator` `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 warnings.
```sh
# DEFECTIVE AS WRITTEN -- do not copy. `eventMessage CONTAINS` matches /usr/bin/log's own
# invocation records, both counters rise together, and this reads outstanding=0 over a standing
# prompt. Use `./scripts/xcb.sh check-automation` (T-2070, corrected 2026-10-07 by `envguard`).
req=$(/usr/bin/log show --last 6h --predicate 'process == "testmanagerd" AND eventMessage CONTAINS "Writer daemon requires authentication"' | grep -c 'Writer daemon requires')
don=$(/usr/bin/log show --last 6h --predicate 'process == "testmanagerd" AND eventMessage CONTAINS "Finished enabling Automation Mode"' | grep -c 'Finished enabling')
outstanding=$((req - don))   # >0 means a prompt is standing and NO macOS test run can work
```

Measured both ways on 2026-10-04: against the healthy host at 15:1x it reads `requests=1 finished=1 outstanding=0`, and against the wedged window (`--start '11:23:00' --end '14:00:00'`, cut before the 14:35:23 release) it reads `requests=1 finished=0 outstanding=1`. It costs **2.2s** and needs no privilege. Do NOT probe for the *"Enable UI Automation"* string alone — that line is still in the log long after the prompt is answered, so it reports a false positive on a healthy host; the pairing is the signal. If one is outstanding, `xcb.sh` should refuse with its own exit code and SAY the owner must authenticate — the same shape as the existing screen-lock refusal, which is the precedent for a preflight that reads host state and declines. **(b) Tell the 445s signature apart from a real failure.** A macOS run whose log reaches *"Received new test session connection"* but never *"requested serialized transport"*, and dies ~445s later with *"The test runner hung before establishing connection"*, is THIS, never a code defect — the zero-test guard currently reports it as an ordinary red and the mutation guard reads a zero-test run as a survivor, which is how a wedged host destroys evidence silently. Note the shell trap when writing the check: a shell function named `log` shadows the binary and makes `log show …` print *"too many arguments"*, so the preflight must call `/usr/bin/log` by absolute path. **Do not "fix" this by disabling automation mode or writing to the authorization database** — that is the line [[T-1742]] and [[T-2049]] already cost someone.

- [T-2059] **CLOSED 2026-10-04 (agent `scrollclaim`) — the tasks page stopped scrolling whenever a drag opened sideways, and no SwiftUI gesture priority could have fixed it: a `DragGesture` on a row cannot hand a touch back to the enclosing `ScrollView` once it has one.** The owner: *"when im on ios, scrolling in the tasks page sometimes doesnt work."* **Reproduced on `Cadence-iPhone15` before anything was changed**, by injecting two drags that differ in nothing but their first three samples. A 168pt drag straight up a task row scrolled the page 157pt. The same drag, from the same point, opening with **14pt of sideways travel** and then running the same 168pt up, scrolled the page **zero** — the screenshots are byte-identical but for the clock. That is the whole of "sometimes": whether the opening points of a thumb's arc happen to be straight. **The cause is this row's own gesture, proved by mutation, twice.** With `.highPriorityGesture(dragGesture, including: .none)` the failing path scrolled; with `including: .subviews` — which disables only the drag and leaves every descendant gesture alive, removing the confound in the first mutation — it scrolled again. **Three candidate fixes were refuted by their own builds, not by argument.** `minimumDistance: 30` stayed dead. `.simultaneousGesture` stayed dead. Claiming the drag *vertical* and returning early out of `onChanged` stayed dead — a drag opening `(4, -13)`, which the old code reads as vertical on its first event, still scrolled nothing. So the file's own comment was **wrong where it mattered**: "It does not contest the enclosing `ScrollView`/`List` pan — that is a separate arbitration" is false, the arbitration is not separate, and the row wins it for any touch whose opening movement is not dead vertical. **The fix is to stop asking SwiftUI to do the one thing it has no word for.** `iOSRowHorizontalPanRecognizer` is a `UIGestureRecognizer` that goes to `.failed` **while it is still `.possible`** when the drag is not horizontal: a recognizer that fails before it begins never asks the scroll view's pan to stand down, so a declined drag scrolls as if the row carried no gesture at all. The decision itself lives in `CadenceSwipeActionSupport.axisClaim`, outside `#if os(iOS)` and therefore pinned by the macOS-built test target, and it reads the axis at a new `CadenceSwipeActionMetrics.claimDistance` of **24pt rather than 12** — measured, not chosen: the reported drag reads *horizontal* at 12 and *vertical* by 24, and a deliberate swipe travels 76pt to open a single action, so waiting for 24 costs it nothing. **The four invariants were each re-measured on the built app, not argued:** vertical scrolling works from a row and from the completion circle; a swipe opens the tray, a tap on an open row closes it, and a 260pt swipe commits the full swipe; a tap on the circle completes, a tap on the row opens Edit Task, and a tap on the estimate chip still opens its popover; and a 163pt swipe begun **on the completion circle** completes nothing. **One regression was found and fixed inside this ticket, and it is the same shape as the bug this container was built to close.** With the recognizer merely added, an identical 260pt swipe committed from the row's text and was *ignored* from the "45m" estimate chip — which sits at the trailing edge, exactly where a right-to-left swipe starts. Letting the two recognize simultaneously fixed that and re-opened the old bug: the swipe opened the tray **and** the chip's popover. The delegate therefore makes the row's controls *wait* for this recognizer (`shouldBeRequiredToFailBy`) and exempts pans, so the scroll view is never made to wait; on a tap there is no movement, the recognizer fails at touch-up, and the control fires as it always did. **The `DragClaim` enum and the `claim` state are gone**, and with them the stale-claim hazard that motivated this investigation: there is no longer a latch to go stale, because the axis is decided per touch by a recognizer UIKit resets itself. **KNOWN, not fixed here:** a vertical drag *begun on the completion circle* scrolls, but measurably less far than the same drag begun on the row's text (≈14pt against ≈67pt for a 152pt finger travel, from downsampled screenshots, so treat the numbers as ordinal). It is an improvement on scrolling nothing, and the cause was not chased. **NOT verified:** iPad, `List`-hosted rows, VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, and real-finger behaviour on hardware — every measurement here is injected touch samples on one simulator, and a real touch stream is smoothed in ways an injected one is not, so the *frequency* the owner experiences may differ from the sharp boundary measured here even though the mechanism does not.

- [T-5500] **OPEN 2026-10-23 (filed by agent `t3219` out of [[T-3041]]; a LIMIT on what an indicator can claim, not a defect in it) -- "records are arriving" is not observable from the mirroring events, so [[T-3041]]'s cold-import notice reads "import passes are still completing" instead.** The owner's [[T-3041]] ruling is to show the indicator only while the import is PROGRESSING -- appear when records are actually arriving, disappear when they stop -- and to say so rather than approximate if the log cannot tell the two apart. It cannot. `CadenceSyncActivityLog` is handed `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer.Event` and nothing else, and that event carries an identifier, a type, a start date, an end date, a success flag and an optional error: **no record count, no progress figure, no object ids**. `CadenceSyncActivityEvent` mirrors exactly those fields (`Cadence/Shared/CadenceSyncActivity.swift`), so a successful import of nine hundred records and a successful import of none are the same value here. [[T-3041]] therefore guards on *a pass succeeded inside the window* plus *another is in flight*, which is a fact about CloudKit's event traffic rather than an inference about its contents, and the source, the tests and the entry all name it as that. **What would close it:** observing `.NSPersistentStoreRemoteChange` (or the merge notification's `NSInsertedObjectIDsKey`) and counting the object ids actually merged into the store, which turns "a pass completed" into "N rows landed". That is a second event source and new plumbing, which is outside what [[T-3041]] was ruled to be -- presentation over a log that already exists -- so it is filed rather than folded in. **Priority is low, and this may not be wanted at all:** the costs of the proxy are the ones the owner already accepted on [[T-3041]] (a slow import may flicker; a stalled one shows nothing), and the proxy never claims more than the events support. Worth deciding only if a restoring tester reports the indicator reading wrongly in practice. Related: [[T-2010]], which is the standing note that nothing here proves Core Data posts these events for a SwiftData store at all.

The sync-driven trigger is DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED, and the reason is not timidity about [[T-2010]]'s delivery doubt — it is that a reconcile is a *removal*, and a removal against a partially imported store cancels real reminders.** RE-CHECKED (agent `sweep2138b`, 2026-10-22, read-only, no test host taken): still PARTIAL as the SHIP-NOTE says -- macOS `NotificationReconcileObserver` reconciles on both arms (`Cadence/macOS/macOSRootView.swift:360-374`); `Cadence/Services/CadenceSyncActivityLog.swift` observes `eventChangedNotification` (`:134`) but has zero `reconcile` hits, and `NotificationManager.shared.reconcile` is called only from `iOSRootView.swift`, `macOSRootView.swift` and `HabitNotificationReconcileSupport.swift` -- the sync-driven trigger is still absent, deliberately. SHIP-NOTE (agent `staleremainder0708b`, 2026-10-22): only the sync-driven reconcile trigger is missing, deliberately -- a reconcile REMOVES every managed request not in the plan, so firing it on a half-imported store cancels real reminders, and nothing in-process can tell a whole store from a partial one; it is fine to ship because both platforms now reconcile on every scene-phase change (macOS `macOSRootView.swift:359-374`, re-read; `CadenceSyncActivityLog` still triggers no reconcile), so a stale queue converges on the next activation and nothing is ever removed on a guess. **The filing was exact.** `NotificationReconcileObserver` guarded its whole closure with `guard phase != .active else { return }` (`Cadence/macOS/macOSRootView.swift:325`), so every becoming-active transition returned before both the widget reload and the reconcile, while iOS's twin ([[T-312]]) reconciles on both arms and gates only the reload. The macOS closure now has exactly the iOS shape: `if phase != .active { reloadAllWidgets() }` with the reconcile outside it. The reload stays on the leaving arm on purpose — it is about what *this* process wrote. **Part (2) HELD, against the very argument the brief put forward.** The brief's asymmetry is right as far as it goes: `lookrace` refused to *gate* a write on `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer.eventChangedNotification` because an undelivered event means the write never happens, whereas *adding* a trigger that sometimes fires beats today's zero triggers. That covers the **failure-to-fire** direction and does not reach the one that bites. `NotificationManager.reconcile` is a converging diff and `NotificationReconcileDiff.make` **removes every managed pending identifier not in `NotificationPlan.build`'s output**, so a sync trigger is not merely a trigger that might not fire — it is a trigger that fires **at a moment whose input may be wrong**, and when the input is a half-imported store the output is cancelled reminders for tasks that have simply not arrived yet. An unreliable trigger is free only when its action is idempotent *upward*; this one is not, and 'no worse off than now' is false for a pass that removes. **The hazard is concrete, and today's own audit is what makes it so.** A pending `UNNotificationRequest` lives in the OS and survives a store replacement, and [[T-3042]]/[[T-3045]] (filed the same day) establish that a failed startup backup drops the launch into an **empty recovery store**. That is exactly the shape — OS queue full, store empty, cold import beginning. A reconcile on the first finished `.import` pass would cancel the lot. Later passes re-add them, because the diff converges, but nothing bounds how long 'later' is: an import stalled on a dropped network or a signed-out account leaves the queue swept with no trigger left to repair it. Whether `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer` posts one finished `.import` per sync or one per batch is a platform fact **not in this tree**, and [[T-2010]] already records that even *delivery* is unestablished without a two-device run. The brief's stop condition therefore applies as written. **The shape it would take, for whoever picks it up.** `CadenceSyncActivityLog.record` already receives every event and `CadenceSyncActivityEvent` carries `phase`, `endDate` (`nil` while running) and `succeeded`, so the trigger needs no second door to CloudKit: `phase == .import`, `endDate != nil`, `succeeded`, trailing-debounced so a burst of passes costs one reconcile. What it needs **first** is an answer to 'is the store whole?', and the only honest candidates are a two-device measurement of the event stream or an additive-only reconcile — and additive-only would not close this ticket, because the defect *is* the removal. **MUTATION-PROVED.** Restoring `guard phase != .active else { return }` **COMPILED** (0 compile errors, 6 Swift tasks, 0 warnings) and turned exactly one test red — `CadenceExternalWriteReconcileTests.macOSReconcilesNotificationsOnEveryScenePhaseChange`, on `!body.contains("guard phase != .active")` (:291) and `body.range(of: "if phase != .active {")` (:298), the direct pin and the structural one. Restored from a `cp` backup in a private `/tmp` dir; `diff -q` identical. **VERIFIED.** 10 suites, **145 tests, `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 compile errors, 0 warnings**, plus the wrapper's iOS leg `COMPILED` clean. The new test is a source scan living beside its iOS twin `iOSReconcilesNotificationsOnEveryScenePhaseChange` rather than in a new file, and it is scoped to `NotificationReconcileObserver`'s own `.onChange` because `macOSRootView` holds a **second** `.onChange(of: scenePhase)` higher up (the external-write refresh, :134) that `cadenceFunctionBody` reaches first. Non-vacuity: the two stripper assertions plus `theSourceScanReachesTheFilesItClaimsTo`, which already listed this file. **NOT VERIFIED.** No notification was scheduled, delivered or cancelled; no device, no simulator, no app launch. `NotificationReconcileObserver` is a private SwiftUI view with `@Environment(.scenePhase)` and an unbounded `@Query`, so there is no symbol to call and every claim here is a claim about the source. Cold launch still reconciles on neither platform — `.onChange` does not fire for the initial value, the hole [[T-2081]] routed around — which is unchanged and is not this ticket. - [T-2050] **OPEN 2026-10-03 (filed by agent `ciattrib` while landing [[T-1993]]) — should an unattributed commit turn CI RED, or stay the notice it is today? The recommendation is KEEP IT A NOTICE, and spend the alarm on the reading where a red is deserved.** [[T-1993]] landed `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `push-attribution` job as a notice: the script exits 1 honestly and the step swallows it. Making it a gate is deleting one `|| rc=$?`. The argument for leaving it alone, in the order that matters. **(1) The red would be false about the code.** `main` is linear, so the tip's tree contains the intermediate commit's bytes and any break is still caught. What a grouped push costs is which commit to blame, not coverage. A job that goes red over a tree that is fine is a different lie from the one T-1950 is about, not the same one fixed. **(2) It is not actionable when it fires.** By the time the step runs, the commits are on `main`. There is nothing the person reading the red can change in the tree to satisfy it; the only remedy is *push differently next time*. A gate nobody can satisfy by editing anything is a gate that gets switched off — the same argument `CI-SKIPPED` and `report`'s deliberate exit 0 are already built on. **(3) The remedy is upstream and behavioural.** T-1950 says so itself: push after each landing. If an alarm is wanted it belongs in the pusher's own loop — `scripts/agent-commit.sh` or the heartbeat, which can refuse BEFORE the group exists — not in the runner that learns about it afterwards. **(4) It would fire constantly today.** The two commits at `main`'s tip on 2026-10-03, `a59379f6..f068a5b9`, already read `UNATTRIBUTED -- 1 of 2`. A gate that is red most of the time teaches people to ignore the colour, and this repository has that failure recorded twice already. **(5) There IS a reading worth a red, and it is a different one.** A code commit that was never pushed at all, or a run cancelled and never replaced, is a COVERAGE failure rather than an attribution one — [[T-1640]]'s `NEVER-PUSHED` and `CANCELLED` over `report`. If the appetite for one more red exists, spend it there. **Decide and record the decision here either way;** the point of filing it is that the notice is a choice someone made with reasons, not the shape the work happened to stop in.

The file's content never changed: `git status` clean, **mtime 2026-09-20 20:18:36 throughout**, while **ctime moved to 2026-10-03 13:29:25** between two runs of the same DerivedData — a metadata-only write (the file carries a `com.apple.provenance` xattr) with the project open in Xcode and sibling agents building the same checkout. Deleting the generated `Cadence.app.xcent` did **not** clear it; `xcb.sh release-dd` plus a fresh full build did, at about 12 minutes. Two things to decide: whether `xcb.sh` should name this when the log matches `Entitlements file .* was modified during the build` — it is one grep, and it turns a four-run dead end into one line — and whether a batch's rule should be that a DerivedData is disposable the moment it fires. Do **not** reach for `CODE_SIGN_ALLOW_ENTITLEMENTS_MODIFICATION=YES`: the error text offers it and it ships a product whose signature may not match its entitlements.

- [T-1840] **Should `Delete Account & Data` delete the recovery store and the earlier store folders? An owner decision, with the reasoning already done.** Filed 2026-09-30 by agent `recoverystore` while closing [[T-1680]], which split the question in two and answered the visible half. The recommendation is **yes**, on `deleteRetainedUnrestoredOriginals`'s own stated tradeoff: that comment keeps a folder out of "clear backups" because it is the last copy of store files a restore could not put back, and sweeps it in the reset because leaving store data inside the container the reset just emptied is the reset claiming more than it did. The second half applies to `Recovery/` verbatim; the first half does not, because `makeRecoveryContainer` does not copy the failed store, it opens an empty one — so a recovery store is not the last copy of anything that exists elsewhere. **Three things this needs that are not obvious.** (1) The sweep must skip the recovery directory when `PersistenceController.startupIssue?.kind == .recoveryStore`: that launch is running **on** that store, and removing the file under an open `ModelContainer` is a different bug. (2) The typed-phrase gate has to name it before the button is live — *"a recovery store Cadence created when it could not open your main one"* — because a recovery store is opened with CloudKit off, so anything typed during that session synced nowhere and this is its only copy; a silent irreversible delete is worse than the silence T-1680 replaced. (3) The earlier store folders are a **separate** decision from the recovery one: they are outside the app's current container, `migrateLegacyStoreIfNeeded` still reads them, and deleting them would make the migration's own fallback unreachable. The row that shows all of them today carries `directory` and `onReveal` and nothing else, on purpose — whatever this ticket decides, the delete does not belong on that row. [[T-1680]] [[T-1100]] [[T-1424]] **OWNER DECISION 2026-10-22 (recorded by the coordinator from the owner's answers in session; no code written yet): YES -- `Delete Account & Data` also deletes the recovery store and the earlier store folders. This adopts the recommendation already reasoned out in this entry. The sweep MUST still skip the recovery directory when `PersistenceController.startupIssue?.kind == .recoveryStore`, because that launch is running on that store.**

- [T-1780] **CLOSED 2026-09-30 (coordinator; filed by agent `padwidth`) — `scripts/simulator-claim.sh claim` hands out the owner's own `iPhone 17 Pro` first, and offers no way to ask for a different device — so the one prohibition its own header states is the one outcome it produces by default.** Found 2026-09-30 by agent `padwidth` on the first claim of the session. The header is unambiguous: "NEVER touch iPhone 17 Pro, 7B642065-86FC-4987-8674-22066D32878C -- that is the owner's own device", and [[T-1704]] added the standing pair above it as what to reuse instead. But `claim` walks `booted_udids()`, which is `xcrun simctl list devices booted` in simctl's own order, and takes the first device it can `mkdir` a claim for. That order is **iPhone 17 Pro, Cadence-iPhone15, iPad Pro 11-inch**, so a plain `./scripts/simulator-claim.sh claim <id> 2700` answered `DEVICE=iPhone 17 Pro` — measured, twice. There is no `--device`/`--name` argument, `CADENCE_SIM_CLAIMS_DIR` is honoured only under `CADENCE_SIM_CLAIM_TESTING`, and `CADENCE_SIMCTL` is a testing seam, so an agent briefed onto the iPad has **no supported route to it at all**. The three unsupported routes an agent will reach for next — a `simctl` wrapper that filters the list, hand-writing the claim directory, or claiming throwaway ids until the allocator walks past the forbidden device — were each tried here and each correctly refused by the permission classifier, which is the right answer and also why this has to be fixed in the script rather than worked around. **Two halves, and the second is the one that matters.** (1) A device selector, so a brief that names a device can be obeyed: `claim <id> [timeout] [--device <name-or-udid>]`, waiting for *that* device rather than any. (2) A **deny list** — the forbidden udid belongs in this script as a constant that `booted_udids` filters out, so the prohibition is enforced by the allocator instead of asserted in a comment above it. Note that `status` already prints the device as `free`, which is the same claim in the other direction. Until both land, the script's header and the script disagree, and the header is the half that is right.


  **The fix.** As filed: `CADENCE_SIM_DENY_UDIDS` is an array the allocator actually reads, and `claim` takes an optional third argument — `iphone` / `ipad` resolve through [[T-1704]]'s standing pair, a bare UDID is taken as-is, and a denied one **exits 2** rather than being quietly substituted. **My first guard for it was VACUOUS and the mutation caught it:** reverting the allocator to its pre-fix body left the new selftest property green, because the fixture's `fake-simctl` printed exactly ONE device — so the allocator never had a choice to get wrong and the property was only exercising the new *selector*. That is the identical mistake to the bug itself, testing the documented intent instead of the allocation. Rewritten so the fixture lists a second fake **first**, standing in for the owner's device, via a `CADENCE_SIM_DENY_EXTRA` hook that is **additive only** — one that could remove an entry would be a way to hand out the owner's device by setting an environment variable. Both polarities asserted; re-mutated and **killed**, the failure naming the denied udid it wrongly allocated. Selftest 5 properties / 0 failures, live `claim` now answers `Cadence-iPhone15`. Thank you for filing it rather than working around it.

- [T-1491] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `filedrop`) — the editor overrode `draggingEntered` and not `draggingUpdated`, so at a host that ACCEPTS images a dragged bitmap got Cadence's copy badge for one frame and AppKit's refusal for the rest of the drag.** Found while measuring [[T-1447]], which is refused above; this is the defect that measurement turned up instead. **The shape.** AppKit calls `draggingEntered` once, as the pointer crosses into the view, and `draggingUpdated` on every movement after that — so `draggingUpdated` is what draws the badge for all but the first frame, and what AppKit reads before it offers `performDragOperation` at all. [[T-478]], [[T-504]], [[T-511]] and [[T-1418]] all reasoned about `draggingEntered` alone and nothing in the app has ever overridden the other one (`rg draggingUpdated Cadence/` → zero hits before this commit). **Measured 2026-09-28, Xcode 27, one windowed `CadenceTextView` after AppKit's own `updateDragTypeRegistration`, one TIFF-only board, `MarkdownDropInfo` driving both calls:** at `allowsMarkdownImageInsertion == true`, `draggingEntered` → **`.copy`** (Cadence's rule) and `draggingUpdated` → **`[]`** (`super`, which refuses a bitmap because `importsGraphics` is off and must stay off — [[T-1418]], `nothingInTheAppTurnsOnImportsGraphics`). Calling `draggingEntered` a second time gave `.copy` again, so the two answers differ by which method was asked and by nothing else. At `allowsMarkdownImageInsertion == false` both gave `[]`, which is why this never showed at a refusing host and why four tickets could pass over it. **It is [[T-478]] with the sign reversed**: that ticket removed a copy badge from an editor that would decline the picture; this is the no-drop cursor over an editor whose whole job is to take it, for the entire time the user is aiming the drop. **The fix is four lines** — `draggingUpdated` now reads the same `markdownImageDropOperation(for:)` and falls through to `super.draggingUpdated`, not `super.draggingEntered`; that distinction matters because the fall-through is the path a plain-text drag takes and `NSTextView`'s two methods do different things to the insertion-point caret. Nothing at a refusing host moves: the rule answers `nil` there, `super` answers both calls, and [[T-1447]]'s deferral is byte-for-byte where it was. **Three tests, none of which asserts anything about AppKit** ([[T-1296]]): `theEditorsDragAnswerIsTheSameOnEntryAndOnEveryMoveAfterIt` asserts the editor's two answers AGREE over a payload its own rule claims — after the fix `super` is consulted by neither, so the equality holds on any toolchain, and what `super` would have said goes into the failure message; `aRefusingHostStillDefersBothDragAnswersToAppKit` asserts the `nil`, which is Cadence's decision, rather than `super`'s verdict, which is [[T-1418]]'s to observe; `bothDragOverridesReadTheSameRuleAndFallThroughToTheirOwnSuper` is the source scan that stops a later edit satisfying the first test by making `draggingUpdated` call `draggingEntered`. **Mutation-proved**, both applied and COMPILED (`compile errors: 0`), both `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=65`, tree restored: dropping the rule from `draggingUpdated` killed `theEditorsDragAnswerIsTheSameOnEntryAndOnEveryMoveAfterIt` (message: *"claimed this drag as 1 when the pointer entered and 0 when it moved"*) and the scan; swapping the fall-through to `super.draggingEntered` killed the scan alone, on both of its assertions — which is the right split, because the behavioural test cannot see it and says so. **Not done:** `draggingExited`, `prepareForDragOperation` and `concludeDragOperation` are still `super`'s, deliberately — Cadence has no opinion to express in any of them, and the rule this commit applies is that an override exists only where the editor's own answer differs from the framework's.

The workflow edits are COMMENTS — no `on:`, `jobs:` or `concurrency:` key or value changed, verified by YAML parse and by the diff — so there is no CI behaviour to observe and none is asserted. With `CadenceTests` at roughly 35 minutes, any burst of three pushes inside one run's window silently drops the middle one. **What to do, none of it decided:** the honest options are to batch pushes while a run is in flight (which reintroduces [[T-1362]]'s blind window and was rejected once), to give the ledger/docs jobs their own concurrency group so a docs-only push cannot displace a code run, or to accept it and make the heartbeat *notice* — a commit whose CI was cancelled currently looks identical to one that was never pushed. **Correct the T-1393 closure and the runbook line together**; a half-true rule in an always-read guide is worse than no rule, and the coordinator wrote this one.

That is real and much smaller, and it changes the remedy: batching pushes to protect coverage would pay [[T-1362]]'s blind window for a benefit that mostly is not there, while making the heartbeat NOTICE a cancelled run stays worth doing. The overstatement is amended rather than edited away, because the reading behind it — counting runs instead of asking what the runs cover — is the shape this ledger keeps catching in its instruments, and this time it was the coordinator's.

- [T-1446] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `countcopy`) — one of the three is a defect and it is the first; the other two are correct as drawn and the arithmetic says so.** **(1) FIXED, and the diagnosis is a question asked one word wrong.** `CadenceEmptyStateCopy.isNarrowedToEmpty` took `filterNarrows`, which answers *is a narrowing filter selected* — true on both pages by default, and `everyDesktopFilterKnowsWhetherItHidesAnything` already pins that Goals opens on *Active* and Habits on *Due Today*. The question the copy needs is *is the filter hiding anything*, and on an empty store the two part company: nothing can be narrowed out of an empty collection. So a reader who had never made a goal or a habit was sent after two controls they had never touched. A third argument, `hasCandidates`, dominates the other two and is answered by the caller, never inferred — "the collection this page draws from" is a different array on each surface and the *filtered* one is empty in exactly the state being asked about. `GoalsView` and `HabitsView` answer from `allGoals` / `habits`; `GoalTimelineView` is handed already-filtered `groups` and so **cannot** answer it, and takes `hasAnyGoal` from `GoalsView` instead. Defaulted to `true`, so the attach-lists sheet — whose `filterNarrows` is already a constant `false` — reads as it did. **(2) CORRECT AS DRAWN, measured.** Both halves the report names are the design, not an accident. `CalendarMonthGridMetrics.rowHeight` is `viewportHeight / weeksInMonth`, so a month block is **exactly one screen tall** and an empty week row is full height by construction; shrinking it would make the row pitch depend on content and break the offset table `CalendarMonthGridSupport.cumulativeOffsets` shares with the renderer, which is the one thing keeping the header from naming a month the grid is not showing. "Opens on the 6th" is `blockFirstDay(of:)`: a block begins on its month's first Sunday and the 0–6 days before it render as trailing fill on the block before, which is how the grid tiles months **without repeating a day** — Sep 1 2026 is a Tuesday, so September's block opens on the 6th. Clipping is possible only under the documented `minimumRowHeight` floor of 72 ("a very short window scrolls instead of shrinking rows into illegibility"), i.e. a grid viewport below `72 × weeks` — **288pt** for September's four rows, **432pt** for a six-row month. - [T-1487] **CLOSED 2026-09-28 (agent `uivalue`) — three fixes were weighed for a UI-level test and exactly ONE earns one, because only one of the three is pinned by a reading that cannot fail the way the owner's screenshot failed.** **The rule this run arrived at, and it is worth more than the test:** *a UI test earns its place here only when the defect is a property of the COMPOSED surface — a frame, a colour, a reachability — and the assertion that already exists is a proxy for that property rather than the property itself.* Three proxies are common in this repository and they rank differently. A **source scan** is the weakest: it asserts the code asks for the right thing, and it is green for every way the right request comes out wrong. A **model/simulator test** is strong where the thing measured is a value the model owns, and it is worth more than a UI test there, because a UI test cannot see model writes at all. A **pixel** reading is weakest of all and is already bounded by `CadenceUITestPixelSupport`. So the bar is not "is there a UI test for this" but "can the UI test fail on an input the existing assertion is green for", and the answer was yes once. **[[T-1432]] — YES, and the test is `CadenceUITests/CadenceTodayRowCrushUITests`.** Its existing pin, `CadenceTasksPanelMetricsTests.theRowsTitleIsLaidOutBeforeItsMetadata`, is a **source scan and says so in its own comment** — *"there is no seam that reports which subview won the width"*. It fails on exactly one event, a deleted modifier, and it is green for every layout those modifiers are present for: `.layoutPriority(1)` **orders** an `HStack`'s allocation and does not guarantee width, so a later `.frame(maxWidth:)`, a `.fixedSize` on a sibling, a padding that grows, or one more chip added outside the `ViewThatFits` all re-crush the title with every needle still in the file — and `.lineLimit(1)` is only one of the two reasons the due chip could come out three lines tall, the other being a width it cannot draw in, which no scan of that chip's body can see. The new test reads **four frames in points** off a window that really laid itself out, and **every figure is a comparison** rather than a threshold, because a width in points is not portable across a font, a display or an Xcode major and this project builds on two ([[T-1279]], [[T-1296]]): a new seed scenario `today-row-crush` plants **two Today rows with titles of the same length**, one carrying the screenshot's decoration (estimate chip, focus control, overdue due chip) and one carrying none, so the assertion is *the decorated row's title is more than half the width the SAME title got with nothing beside it* — about **0.1** in the owner's photograph. Three more readings come free and each fails on something the first cannot: the due chip's box measured **in title-lines** (a wrap is ~3, a correct chip is under 1); the decorated row's HEIGHT against the bare row's, which is the same fact from the row's side and is the only reading left if a row ever clips a wrapped chip instead of growing; and chip-past-the-row-edge / chip-over-the-title, which catch the fix's own failure mode in the other direction. Non-vacuity is asserted, not assumed: the decorated title must be **strictly narrower** than the bare one (or nothing is trailing it and the fixture has stopped crowding anything) and the bare title must be **narrower than its own row** (or the seeded title fits and there is no pressure to divide). **It clicks, drags and hovers nothing** — the app launches to `.today` — so unlike the two existing composed-window tests it is NOT behind the interactive opt-in and runs in every UI run. **[[T-1431]] — NO, and the reason is not cost.** What was fixed is a **count of model writes**, and XCUITest cannot observe a model write; the only thing it could observe is the value the roller lands on, which was never wrong. The existing pin is also not a source scan: `EstimateRollerMetricsTests` drives a **real `EstimateRollerCommitGate`** through a real live-scroll transcript and states the before number (11 writes) beside the after (1), which is strictly better evidence than a UI test could produce. The unmeasured half — *"it feels smooth"* — stays unmeasured, and a UI test would not have measured it either: `XCUIScreenshot` samples on demand, not per frame, which is the same reason [[T-1068]] leaves Today's flicker unpinned. **[[T-1433]] — NO, and this is the closest call**, because its pins are almost entirely source scans and a source scan cannot prove a surface is REACHABLE or that its fields are DRAWN. It still does not clear the bar: the realistic failure a scan misses here is content clipped out of a fixed popover, and the popover has no fixed height — `QuickCreateChoicePopover` frames `width` only and the form carries `minHeight`, so it grows to its content. Against that, a UI test would have to add product identifiers to an unidentified timeline canvas, synthesise the drag that opens the popover, and then assert *four rows exist* — which is the scan restated somewhere slower and flakier. Two things are recorded rather than done: a macOS popover is **its own `NSWindow`**, so `window.screenshot()` of the main window cannot see it at all and the pixel group is not merely expensive here but blind; and the one defect a UI test could uniquely catch in this area — a child picker popover occluding the composer that opened it — is **[[T-1480]]**'s, not this fix's, and it is expressible as GEOMETRY (two popover frames that overlap) rather than as pixels, which is worth knowing before anyone builds a fixture for it. **On [[T-1449]] and [[T-1480]] as a class:** a planted-fixture pixel invariant can catch a translucent fill (a known flat colour is no longer that colour) but it needs a saturated fixture inside the surface under test, and the only one that exists is an image in a note. Putting one inside a popover means test-only colour in product code; that is the line, and this run did not cross it. **No golden image was added and none should be.** **Verified:** scoped `CadenceTests` run over the five suites this change touches — `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, **100** result lines, 0 failures, **0** warnings, **1068** swift compile tasks; and `build-for-testing` of the UI target, `XCODEBUILD_EXIT=0`, 0 errors, **0** warnings, with `CadenceTodayRowCrushUITests.swift` confirmed in the compile log so the count is not vacuous. **NOT VERIFIED, and it is the point of [[T-1488]]:** the new test has **never executed**. `scripts/xcb.sh` refused the UI run twice with *"the screen is locked"* — the [[T-563]] switch — and the brief's instruction was to report that and stop rather than retry in a loop. Nothing here claims a green UI run, and the two bounds in the test are labelled **not measured** in their own doc comments rather than given numbers invented after the fact, which is this target's existing rule for `CadenceUITestBounds`. **Product changes are two accessibility identifiers and one seed scenario, all inert.** `task.row.<slug>.title` and `task.row.<slug>.due` go on `MacTaskRow` — spelled `task.row.` and not `today.task.row.` because `MacTaskRow` has one call site that Today and a list's detail pane both draw from, so the `today.` prefix would be false on half its occurrences, and the test scopes its query to the row element instead. The title needs an identifier for a reason the defect itself supplies: **a truncated title is not addressable by its text**, so a lookup by label would stop resolving at the exact moment the defect appeared and report *"no such element"* where the finding is *"it is 70pt wide"*. `CadenceAgentDefaultsIsolationTests`' launch-site count goes 4 → 5 with the new file named, which is that test doing what it was written to do.

- [T-1611] **One Task tab or two: the product question [[T-1435]] framed, kept after its refactor premise was refuted.** Filed 2026-09-29 by agent `composers` on closing T-1435 and [[T-1436]]. A Swift diagnostic is not one line: the snippet renderer prints the primary `file:LINE:COL: warning:` line and then repeats the whole message on a caret continuation inside the snippet, `` |   `- warning: 'zzDeprecated()' is deprecated ``. Same shape as the ticket's own captured 2026-09-29 logs (6 loose over 3 macro-expansion diagnostics → `tool notices: 3`, true count 0). It never gated, by design ([[T-1147]]), so this is a readability defect — and the reader it misleads is precisely the one triaging a run that HAS diagnostics. **What shipped:** a third pattern beside the other two, `CONTINUATION_WARNING_PATTERN`, whose value is the caret form `` `- warning: ``, and `notices` recomputed as a SET DIFFERENCE — `grep 'warning:' "$log" | grep -vcE "$SWIFT…|$MACRO…|$CONTINUATION…"` — rather than as `loose - warnings - continued`. Arithmetic was the wrong shape for a reason worth keeping: if a line ever matched two patterns at once the subtraction goes NEGATIVE and the banner prints nonsense, while a set difference cannot. **Both warning patterns and the gating total are untouched**: `warnings:` and the exit code are byte-identical before and after on every fixture and on a real 1,094-task run, which is why every clean run (the normal case, zero warnings) reads exactly as it did. **The marker is `` `- `` and nothing else, and that was looked for rather than assumed:** six real diagnostics across three `swiftc -typecheck` probes on this toolchain, plus the two captured 2026-09-29 logs, print this continuation marker and no other; `|- warning:` was grepped for in all of them and never seen, so it is deliberately NOT matched — an unwitnessed alternative is a pattern this repository cannot show a line for, and missing one would only restore today's inflation rather than break a count. **Every other site that counts notices, enumerated by search and not by memory** ([[T-1328]]'s lesson, the way [[T-1516]] did it): `scripts/xcb.sh` is the ONLY one. `.github/scripts/check-log.sh` prints `swift warnings (strict)` plus the macro subtotal and has no notice reading at all; `scripts/mutate.sh`'s `COMPILE_WARNING`/`MACRO_WARNING` count warnings only, report-only, and never subtract; `ci.yml` and `docs.yml` own no warning grep. Nothing else to fix — said out loud because an empty list that was never searched reads exactly like one that was. **Guards, and the fixture IS the argument.** `xcb.sh selftest` goes 84 → **90 checks**. The new fixture carries both halves at once, which is the only shape that can see this: a log with one notice and no diagnostics passes with the defect fully intact (`loose - warnings` is right whenever there is nothing to continue — which is exactly why `notice.log` and `toolnoise.log`, both already present, never caught it), and a log with diagnostics and no notices is equally satisfied by a counter hard-wired to zero. So it is two real diagnostics (four `warning:` lines, two of them continuations, captured fresh from `swiftc`) beside two real notices, and the load-bearing check is a RELATION rather than a figure: deleting the diagnostics must leave the notice count UNCHANGED and non-zero. In Swift, `CadenceBuildInvocationHygieneTests.theRunnersNoticeCountReadsADiagnosticsContinuationAsPartOfTheDiagnostic` lifts the new pattern out of the script and runs it through `NSRegularExpression` over the real witnesses in both directions — 2 on the fresh continuation block, 1 on the macro block, and **0** on `ld:`, on `actool:`, on the AppIntents notice, on a primary `.swift:N:C:` line (already subtracted as a warning, so a pattern matching both would subtract it twice) and on the attached-macro line that has no continuation — then reads the script's own arithmetic: the variable is recovered FROM THE BANNER THAT PRINTS IT rather than pinned by name, and its assignment must reference the continuation pattern, which is the half that a pattern declared and never used would pass. **Mutated four times, every one killed, each named.** (1) `notices=$(( loose - warnings ))` restored verbatim — `xcb.sh selftest` **86/4**, killing *"…and their caret continuations are NOT reported as tool notices"* (reported 4, right answer 2), *"…and the SAME two notices alone read the same: adding diagnostics changes nothing"* (with: 4, without: 2), and both macro-continuation checks. (2) the minimal one — the pattern left declared but dropped from the `grep -v` alternation — the same 4 die, so it is the SUBTRACTION doing the work and not the refactor. (3) `CONTINUATION_WARNING_PATTERN` widened to plain `warning:`, the mutation that zeroes the counter out — **86/4**, and the two that die are [[T-1147]]'s own CONTROLS (*"but it is still reported, as a tool notice"*, *"…and all three are still reported as tool notices rather than dropped"*) plus the relation's non-zero clause: the link and asset notices this banner exists to keep cannot be swallowed. A `git reset` in the shared checkout is what is on the other side of that. **Measured, minimally, rather than reasoned about.** A three-line `victim.zsh` that `cp`s a 40-line-longer file over itself prints its own remaining lines and then EXECUTES all 40 of the replacement's; the same script using `cp` to a temp and `mv -f` over itself prints its three lines and stops. `mv` is a rename, so the running shell keeps the OLD inode and the new content only reaches the next invocation. **The fix is that one substitution** in step 5b — write the staged content to `$scratch/<key>.resync` and `mv -f` it into place — which is also atomic for every other reader of that path, not just for self-committal. **Why it has never been seen**: it needs `scripts/agent-commit.sh` to be one of the committed paths AND the commit to change its length AND the worktree copy to differ from the staged content, which is exactly the shape of a commit that edits this script, and those commits have until now shrunk or barely moved it. **A selftest for it must not run inside the script's own process** — the fixture has to commit a COPY of `agent-commit.sh` from a throwaway repository, which is how every other mode already drives it. **Follow-up, same day, and the lesson is the coordinator's:** the first fix declared `local resync_tmp` and `local resync_mode` INSIDE the re-sync loop, so the declaration is reached once per iteration — exactly what `noZshScriptReachesABareLocalDeclarationTwice` refuses. It passed `agent-commit.sh selftest` (284/284) and reddened CI, because the script's own selftest does not carry that scan and the Swift suite that does was not run. Declarations hoisted beside `wt_previous`; both instruments green afterwards (284/284, and `CadenceGuardScriptSelftestTests` at 1,047 compile tasks). This is the same class as [[T-1362]] and [[T-1385]] a third time: a green scoped run is evidence about the suites you chose, and the guard that would have caught you is the one you did not think to pick.

  **The scroll rule is one function with three rungs**, `CadenceScheduleSupport.initialTimelineHour`: the first timed item, else the current hour backed off an hour when today is on screen, else the work-hours start. The three edge cases the brief asked for, decided and pinned. **(a) A day with nothing timed** falls through to the rungs that were already there; on macOS the remembered hour sits between them, so an empty day still opens where the user left it. **(b) A first item at 23:00** opens at 22:00 — `timelineHour(forFirstTimedMinute:)` clamps to `calendarEndHour - 1` and the scroll view clamps the offset to the foot of its content, so the block lands at the bottom of the viewport rather than off it.   **The two platforms do not share a scroll mechanism and were not made to.** iOS derives an offset and asserts it through a `ScrollPosition` once the canvas reports a content height; macOS restores a *persisted* `calendarRememberedTimelineHour` through a `ScrollViewProxy` id. So what is shared is the arithmetic, not the plumbing: `CalendarPageStateSupport.restoredTimelineHour` calls the same `initialTimelineHour`, and `bothPlatformsOpenTheSameDayAtTheSameHour` holds the two answers equal by construction rather than by two rules that currently agree — which is the drift [[T-596]] and [[T-1129]] are in the ledger for. **The first rung outranks macOS's remembered hour, and that has a real cost:** a user who scrolled to 14:00, left the page and came back now lands on the day's first block instead of at 14:00. It is the owner's sentence read literally, and the alternative keeps the complaint alive, since a remembered hour is written from wherever a scroll happened to stop rather than from a choice. Pinned in `theFirstTimedItemOutranksTheRememberedTimelineHour`, so reversing it is a decision and not a drift.

Any week within a fortnight of today therefore answered "shows today" and opened at the current hour, and at 1 AM the current hour is the top of the canvas. That is the owner's week, and no amount of first-timed-item logic would have fixed it on a span with nothing on it. It asks `CadenceCalendarTimelineWindow.visibleDates` now — the columns actually on screen — and `theVisibleSpanIsTheColumnsOnScreenNotTheEventFetchWindow` states the difference.
